topic: Whole-Body Perfusion: Total vs Partial CPB
stem: During CPB, some systemic venous blood is allowed to return to the right atrium, pass through the lungs, and be ejected by the left ventricle into the aorta. This **partial CPB** has long been known to be better tolerated than total CPB. What is the **most likely explanation**?

choices.text: Lower nonphysiologic shear stress in the arterial pump
Continuation of at least some pulmonary blood flow
Elimination of blood contact with nonendothelial surfaces
Avoidance of systemic heparin anticoagulation
Need for a lower total perfusion flow rate

explanation.text: Partial CPB is better tolerated than total CPB; the reasons are not clearly defined, but ==continued pulmonary blood flow== is the likely explanation.

head: Total CPB
Partial CPB
rows: **Some** returns to the right atrium and right ventricle
Blood passes the lungs -> left atrium -> **left ventricle ejects** into the aorta

explanation.text: The body is unaccustomed to the **absence of any appreciable pulmonary blood flow** and to only minimally pulsatile aortic pressure, two abnormalities of total CPB.

explanation.title: Used on purpose
explanation.text: During cooling and rewarming, partial CPB produces some arterial pulsation **and some pulmonary blood flow, with its favorable effect**.
Partial CPB has long been known to be better tolerated than total CPB. Reasons for this have not been clearly defined, but continuation of at least some pulmonary blood flow is a likely explanation.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 43

choiceNotes.a: Shear stress is one of the general complexities of CPB; it is not the explanation offered for the better tolerance of partial CPB.
choiceNotes.c: In partial CPB part of the systemic venous blood still passes through the pump-oxygenator, so foreign-surface contact continues.
choiceNotes.d: The patient is anticoagulated with heparin **before CPB is established**; this is not what distinguishes partial CPB.
choiceNotes.e: Flow rate is not offered as the reason; the likely explanation is ongoing **pulmonary blood flow**.

stem: During CPB, virtually all humoral and cellular components of the inflammatory response are **acutely activated**. What is the **principal cause** of this activation?

choices.text: Systemic hypothermia during the perfusion period
Hemodilution of plasma albumin by the priming fluid
Loss of pulsatile aortic pressure during bypass
Blood passage across nonendothelial foreign surfaces
Systemic heparin anticoagulation before bypass

explanation.text: Blood has always passed through **endothelium-lined channels**; during CPB it crosses ==nonendothelial foreign surfaces==, which the organism recognizes as “nonself,” and inflammation is activated.

steps.label: activates
steps.text: Virtually **all humoral and cellular** components of inflammation (and probably some specific immune responses, at least initially)

explanation.text: Other things blood does **not naturally** do on CPB: contain **gaseous and particulate emboli** and experience **nonphysiologic shear stresses**. The general **stress response** of surgery and trauma also occurs to a major degree.

explanation.title: Why it matters after surgery
explanation.text: These features make the patient who has undergone CPB a **unique organism, at least for a few days**; a detailed knowledge of the post-CPB state is necessary for optimal postoperative care.
Throughout evolution, blood has passed only through channels lined with endothelial cells, but during CPB, it is passed across nonendothelial foreign surfaces.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 43

choiceNotes.a: Hypothermia of even moderate degree appears to **blunt** some of the damaging effects of CPB.
choiceNotes.b: Hemodilution lowers colloid osmotic pressure and favors fluid shift into the interstitium; it is not the cited trigger of inflammation.
choiceNotes.c: Minimally pulsatile pressure is a separate abnormality of CPB; inflammatory activation is attributed to **foreign-surface contact**.
choiceNotes.e: Heparin is given to anticoagulate the patient; activation is linked to blood recognizing foreign surfaces as **“nonself.”**

stem: During total CPB, physiologic variables fall into groups according to who controls them. Which variable is **directly controlled externally** by the perfusion team?

choices.text: Temperature of the perfusate
Systemic vascular resistance
Total body oxygen consumption
Mixed venous oxygen levels
Lactic acidemia and pH

explanation.text: Perfusate (and patient) **temperature** is one of the variables ==under direct external control== during total CPB.

explanation.caption: Three groups of variables during total CPB
head: Group
Examples
rows: Total systemic blood flow (“cardiac” output); input pressure waveform; systemic venous pressure; pulmonary venous pressure; hematocrit and chemistry of the initial perfusate; arterial O~2~, CO~2~ and nitrogen levels; temperature of perfusate and patient
Systemic vascular resistance; total body VO~2~; mixed venous O~2~ levels; lactic acidemia and pH; regional and organ blood flow; organ function
All components of **inflammation**, incited by foreign surfaces recognized as “nonself”

explanation.title: Classic confusion
explanation.text: Flow and temperature are **set**; resistance, oxygen consumption and venous oxygen levels are **responses** of the patient.
During total CPB, many physiologic variables are under direct external control, in contrast to the situation in intact humans.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 43

choiceNotes.b: Systemic vascular resistance is determined only **in part** by the controlled variables and **in large part by the patient**.
choiceNotes.c: Total body oxygen consumption belongs to the group determined in large part by the patient.
choiceNotes.d: Mixed venous oxygen levels are determined in large part by the patient, not set directly.
choiceNotes.e: Lactic acidemia and pH are partly determined by the controlled variables but largely by the patient.

topic: Controlled Variables: Arterial Output to the Patient
stem: An arterial **roller pump** has been adjusted so that it is **too nonocclusive**. What is the main consequence?

choices.text: Trauma to the formed elements of blood is increased
Its output becomes markedly pulsatile
Its stroke volume rises during hypothermia
Its arterial line pressure is capped at about 500 mmHg
Its flow is not maintained as resistance varies

explanation.text: A roller pump that is too nonocclusive is ==unable to maintain the same flow== against the wide range of resistances (pressure differentials of **30–300 mmHg**) from the arterial cannula and systemic vascular resistance.

head: Setting
Consequence
rows: More trauma to the formed elements of blood
Cannot maintain the same flow against the range of resistances

explanation.title: How it is set
explanation.text: With the pump-oxygenator fully primed, the system is pressurized to **300 mmHg** on an onboard manometer and the roller heads are adjusted to allow a **slight pressure drop over 1 minute**.

explanation.title: Tubing in the cold
explanation.text: During hypothermia **Tygon** tubing decreases in elasticity and filling volume (stroke volume slightly falls); **silicone rubber** tubing does not, so it may be used in the pump head when hypothermia is required.
When they are occlusive, trauma to the formed elements in blood is increased; when they are too nonocclusive, they are unable to maintain the same rate of flow against the wide range of resistances
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.a: Increased trauma to formed elements occurs when roller pumps are **occlusive**.
choiceNotes.b: The roller pump generates a **relatively nonpulsatile** flow.
choiceNotes.c: During hypothermia, Tygon tubing loses elasticity and filling volume, so stroke volume slightly **decreases**.
choiceNotes.d: A pressure ceiling of about 500 mmHg with line occlusion is a feature of the **controlled vortex** pump.

stem: A controlled vortex (centrifugal) pump is used as the arterial pump. Why must an **ultrasonic flow meter** be placed on the arterial or venous line?

choices.text: Its output is pulsatile, so the console cannot average the flow
It is set nearly occlusive, so tubing wear alters its output
Its flow varies with inflow and outflow resistance at a given rpm
Its tubing stiffens in hypothermia and reduces its stroke volume
It cannot transmit air, so bubble detection relies on the meter

explanation.text: In contrast to the roller pump, ==rpm of the controlled vortex pump cannot be used to estimate flow==, because its flow varies with resistance to inflow and outflow; an **ultrasonic flow meter** is required.

steps.text: Resistance into or out of the pump changes

steps.label: so

explanation.title: Also used for
explanation.text: Closed-chest support with central or peripheral arterial and venous cannulation, termed **cardiopulmonary support (CPS)**.
Therefore, in contrast to the roller pump, revolutions per minute (rpm) of the controlled vortex pump cannot be used to estimate flow.

choiceNotes.b: The occlusion setting applies to the **roller** pump; the vortex pump is **nonocclusive**.
choiceNotes.d: That describes **Tygon tubing in a roller pump head**.
choiceNotes.e: Like the roller pump, the vortex pump **can transmit air bubbles** from the venous to the arterial lines.

stem: During CPB with a controlled vortex (centrifugal) arterial pump, the arterial line is **accidentally clamped completely**. What happens?

choices.text: Flow continues, and line pressure rises until a connector gives way
Flow continues at the set rate because the pump speed is unchanged
Flow stops at once, and line pressure then rises without limit
Flow stops at once, and line pressure rises no higher than about 500 mmHg
Flow stops only when inflow line pressure falls to about −500 mmHg

explanation.text: With a vortex pump, complete arterial line occlusion makes ==flow cease immediately==, but line pressure rises **no higher than about 500 mmHg**, so tubing rupture or connector failure is unlikely.

explanation.caption: Built-in limits of the controlled vortex pump
head: Situation
Result
rows: Output line pressure reaches about **500 mmHg**
Inflow line pressure falls to about **−500 mmHg**

explanation.title: Safety
explanation.text: This pressure ceiling is why it is **unlikely that the tubing will rupture or a junction connector will give way**.
If the arterial line becomes completely occluded, either intentionally or by accident, flow immediately ceases, but pressure in the arterial line will rise no higher than 500 mmHg.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.a: Because pressure rises no higher than about 500 mmHg, it is **unlikely** that the tubing will rupture or a connector give way.
choiceNotes.b: Vortex-pump flow varies with resistance; with complete occlusion **flow immediately ceases**.
choiceNotes.c: Pressure in the arterial line rises **no higher than 500 mmHg**.
choiceNotes.e: That describes obstruction on the **inflow** side; complete outflow occlusion stops flow immediately.

stem: Which statement correctly compares how the controlled vortex pump and the roller pump handle **air**?

choices.text: Air in a vortex pump breaks into microbubbles; a roller pump will pump gross air
A vortex pump cannot transmit air bubbles to the arterial line
A roller pump breaks air into microbubbles; a vortex pump pumps gross air
Air causes far more blood trauma in the vortex pump than in a roller pump
A vortex pump traps air, so its flow can be estimated from rpm

explanation.text: Air entrapped in a vortex pump ==breaks down into microbubbles== that eventually pass out of the pump, whereas a **roller pump will pump gross air** presented to it, with potentially disastrous consequences.

explanation.title: Do not over-trust the vortex pump
explanation.text: It still **can transmit air bubbles** from the venous to the arterial lines.
air entrapped in a vortex pump breaks down into microbubbles that eventually pass out of the pump; a roller pump will pump gross air presented to it with potentially disastrous consequences.

choiceNotes.c: This is reversed: it is the **roller** pump that pumps gross air presented to it.
choiceNotes.d: Blood trauma is **similar** in controlled vortex and roller pumps.
choiceNotes.e: Vortex-pump rpm **cannot** be used to estimate flow; a flow meter is needed.

stem: A regulated and monitored vacuum is applied to the venous reservoir, and a **roller pump** is used as the arterial pump. What is the **most important** advantage of this arrangement?

choices.text: It eliminates microemboli at any vacuum level
It allows the venous reservoir to be removed from the circuit
Output and input pressures can be varied independently
Venous negative pressure rises automatically if the cannula is occluded
It requires larger venous cannulae but less priming volume

explanation.text: A regulated vacuum on the venous reservoir is the **ideal** method of venous drainage; most importantly, with an arterial roller pump the ==output and input pressures are uncoupled== and can be varied independently.

explanation.center: Regulated vacuum on the venous reservoir

children: Patient and machine at about the same level
Negative pressure does not exceed the set level if the cannula occludes
Negative pressure can be varied as needed
Arterial and venous pressures uncoupled (roller pump)

explanation.title: With a vortex arterial pump
explanation.text: The venous vacuum **reduces the outflow pressure** of the nonocclusive vortex pump, so **higher rpm** is needed to keep flow constant.
Most importantly, the two pressures (i.e., output pressure to the patient and input pressure from the patient) are uncoupled and can be varied independently with an arterial roller pump.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.a: The disadvantage of VAVR is a **potential increase in microemboli** at higher vacuum settings.
choiceNotes.b: VAVR uses a **hard-shelled venous reservoir** with a vacuum regulator.
choiceNotes.d: With a regulated vacuum the negative pressure **does not rise above the controlled level** if the cannula becomes occluded.
choiceNotes.e: VAVR permits **smaller** venous cannulae (and smaller reservoirs, shorter tubing, low prime).

stem: For a cardiac operation through a small incision, the team plans **vacuum-assisted venous return** (VAVR) using a hard-shelled venous reservoir and a vacuum regulator on wall suction. Which is the recognized **disadvantage** of this technique?

choices.text: Need for larger venous cannulae
Larger circuit priming volume
Lower hematocrit during bypass
Greater use of blood products
More microemboli at high vacuum

explanation.text: The disadvantage of VAVR is a ==potential increase in microemboli at higher vacuum settings==.
Typical setup: a **hard-shelled venous reservoir** plus a vacuum regulator on wall suction set at **−40 to −60 cm H~2~O**.

explanation.title: Where it helps most
explanation.text: Smaller cannulae, smaller reservoirs, shorter tubing and low prime make VAVR of considerable value in **infants** and for operations **through small incisions** in children and adults.
The disadvantage of VAVR is a potential increase in microemboli at higher vacuum settings.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.a: VAVR permits **smaller** venous cannulae.
choiceNotes.b: VAVR **reduced** priming volume (2.0 ± 0.4 L to 1.4 ± 0.4 L in the Cleveland Clinic study).
choiceNotes.c: VAVR **increased** hematocrit both on bypass and immediately postbypass.
choiceNotes.d: VAVR **reduced** blood product use (from 39% to 19% of patients).

stem: During vacuum-assisted venous return, a ventricular drainage catheter attached to a roller pump rotating at high rpm is suddenly removed from the heart, pulling a large volume of air into the hard-shelled venous reservoir. If the reservoir is **not adequately vented**, what is the danger?

choices.text: The vacuum rises without limit and collapses the venae cavae
Blood and then a column of air can be pushed up the venous line into the heart
The arterial roller pump output falls because the pressures are coupled
A vortex arterial pump delivers gross air into the aorta
Sudden severe hemodilution from the vent circuit

explanation.text: A sudden increase of air into an inadequately vented hard-shell reservoir can ==push blood followed by a column of air up the venous return tubing and into the heart==.

steps.text: Vent on a roller pump at **high rpm** is removed

steps.label: pulls
steps.text: Large volume of **air** into the hard-shell reservoir

steps.label: drives
steps.text: Blood, then a **column of air**, retrograde up the venous line **into the heart**

explanation.title: Safeguards that resulted
explanation.text: Such complications have occurred; they led to **alarms that detect positive reservoir pressure** and **one-way (duckbill) valves** that relieve it.
If the air pulled into the venous reservoir is not adequately vented, it can push blood followed by a column of air up the venous return tubing and into the heart.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.a: With a regulated vacuum the negative pressure does not rise above the controlled level; the danger here is **positive** reservoir pressure.
choiceNotes.c: With an arterial roller pump, venous and arterial pressures are **uncoupled** under VAVR.
choiceNotes.d: Air entrapped in a vortex pump **breaks down into microbubbles**; the described danger is retrograde air up the venous line.
choiceNotes.e: The danger described is **positive reservoir pressure** driving air retrograde, not hemodilution.

choices.text: It is complex, unreliable, and expensive
It works only with 18F to 20F venous cannulae
It generates a very wide range of negative pressures
It is unaffected by large boluses of air in the venous line
Its reservoir increases the priming volume

explanation.text: Most importantly, siphon drainage needs a ==reservoir, which increases the priming volume==; it is otherwise simple, reliable, effective, and inexpensive.

stem: A normal-sized adult is placed on support through **percutaneous peripheral cannulation**, with a controlled vortex pump drawing directly from the venous line. Which venous cannula is appropriate, and why?

choices.text: A 28F–32F cannula, as is needed for gravity drainage
The largest cannula that fits snugly in the vena cava
A small cannula of some length, placing resistance between pump and tip
A small cannula, because a vortex pump cannot create negative pressure
A large cannula, so resistance lies between the cannula tip and the cava

explanation.text: With venous pumping, ==small venous cannulae== put the resistance between the pump and the cannula tip, controlling the gradient that would otherwise make the right atrial or caval walls **“flutter”** around the cannula end.

steps.text: Vortex pump creates a **large pressure gradient**

steps.label: uncontrolled at the tip
steps.text: Caval or atrial walls **“flutter”** around the cannula

steps.label: solution
steps.text: **Small cannula** -> resistance between pump and tip

steps.label: bonus
steps.text: Adequate drainage through a **small percutaneous cannula of some length** (p. 45: 18F or 20F in a normal-sized adult); facilitates **minimally invasive** surgery

explanation.text: One way of accomplishing this is to use small venous cannulae to impose considerable resistance between the pump and tip of the cannula rather than between the tip of the cannula and the patient’s venous system.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 45

choiceNotes.a: 28F–32F catheters are required for **gravity** drainage; with venous pumping, small cannulae are used.
choiceNotes.b: Venous cannulae should lie **loosely, not snugly**; with venous pumping a small cannula is used deliberately.
choiceNotes.d: A controlled vortex pump **can create negative pressure** within the venous line; the small cannula is chosen to control the gradient at the tip.
choiceNotes.e: The aim is the opposite: resistance should lie **between the pump and the cannula tip**, not between the tip and the patient’s venous system.

choices.text: The roller pump head, because of compression by the rollers
The oxygenator, because of its large blood–surface contact
The arterial cannula, because of jet flow at its tip
The heat exchanger, because of its high water temperature
The venous reservoir, because of blood stasis

steps.label: so
steps.text: The **boundary layer** of blood is made very large in the oxygenator

steps.label: therefore
steps.text: Most blood–surface contact, and **most blood damage**, occurs there

items: Regulates **gas tensions** in the arterial blood leaving the pump-oxygenator
By contrast, only a **small proportion** of blood elements contacts tubing and pump surfaces

choiceNotes.c: Cannula gradients matter at high flow, but the **oxygenator** is identified as the main site of blood damage.

stem: Before CPB, a patient receives heparin 300–400 units/kg. **Virtually all** of heparin’s anticoagulant activity is due to which action?

Binding to and greatly amplifying antithrombin III
Chelating ionized calcium, like citrate
Preventing contact activation of factor XII
Acting as a peptide analog of hirudin

explanation.title: Bovine lung heparin

stem: A 66-year-old man has received intravenous heparin for several days before urgent coronary surgery. After the usual heparin dose for CPB, the **ACT remains well below target**, although the measured **plasma heparin concentration is in the usual range**. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
Use of porcine rather than bovine lung heparin
Contact activation of factor XII by the circuit
An inadequate plasma heparin concentration
Antithrombin deficiency from previous heparin exposure

explanation.text: Heparin levels usually correlate with ACT; the exception is ==antithrombin deficiency==, a state of heparin resistance, most commonly caused by **previous heparin exposure** (dose dependent).

explanation.title: Do not trust the heparin level alone
explanation.text: In antithrombin deficiency the heparin level can look adequate while the ACT shows inadequate anticoagulation.

choiceNotes.b: Porcine heparin is the current standard; bovine lung heparin differed in its **protamine neutralization** response.
choiceNotes.c: Factor XII activation is the **subclinical coagulation** seen in most patients on CPB; it is not heparin resistance.
choiceNotes.d: The measured heparin concentration is in the **usual range**; the ACT and heparin level have diverged.

Replace heparin with bivalirudin
Add tranexamic acid to the pump prime
Supplement antithrombin with FFP or concentrate
Monitor the heparin concentration instead of the ACT

Hypothermia lowers blood viscosity, so fewer red cells are needed
A low hematocrit protects the brain during low-flow CPB
A higher hematocrit prevents red cell aggregation in the cold
Hypothermia raises viscosity; a lower hematocrit aids microcirculation

explanation.text: **TP10** (soluble complement receptor type 1) inhibited complement activation in high-risk patients but gave **no consistent improvement in outcome**; it is not approved for CPB.
These agents do not appear to reduce complement activation, but there is evidence to support the hypothesis that they attenuate complement-mediated leukocyte activation
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 48

choiceNotes.a: Corticosteroids **do not appear to reduce complement activation**.
choiceNotes.b: Corticosteroids **lessen** the increase in extracellular water that usually accompanies CPB.
choiceNotes.c: Some studies report improved clinical status, but the matter **remains controversial**.
choiceNotes.d: Osmotic diuresis is provided by **mannitol**.

Ultrafiltration during cooling to raise the hematocrit early
Ultrafiltration only late in CPB if hematocrit is below 0.25 with excess volume
Avoiding ultrafiltration and adding balanced electrolyte solution
Ultrafiltration only after all cannulae have been removed

topic: Changes During CPB: Total Systemic Blood Flow
stem: A 95-kg man with a body surface area of **2.2 m^2^** undergoes CPB at a nasopharyngeal temperature of **34°C**. Which perfusion flow may be chosen, and why?

choices.text: 2.5 L/min/m^2^, as for any patient at 28°C or more
2.2 L/min/m^2^, because higher flow improves oxygenator performance
1.0 L/min/m^2^, as is adequate at 18°C–20°C
1.8–2.0 L/min/m^2^, to avoid high flow through the oxygenator
3.0 L/min/m^2^, to match his larger body size

explanation.text: For adults with a BSA of **2.0 m^2^ or more**, a flow of ==1.8–2.0 L/min/m^2^== may be chosen to avoid the disadvantage of **high flow through the oxygenator**.

items: More **gaseous emboli** with a bubble oxygenator
Larger **pressure gradient across the arterial cannula** -> cavitation, blood trauma, bubbles

explanation.text: For adults with a body surface area of 2.0 m^2^ or more, a flow of 1.8 to 2.0 L · min^-1^ · m^-2^ may be chosen to avoid the disadvantage of high flow through the oxygenator.

choiceNotes.a: 2.5 L/min/m^2^ is usually chosen for **infants and children younger than about 4 years**.
choiceNotes.b: High flow is a **disadvantage** for the oxygenator: blood trauma there is probably greater with high flows.
choiceNotes.c: Flows of 1 L/min/m^2^ are adequate for prolonged periods at **18°C–20°C**, not at 34°C.
choiceNotes.e: Larger adults (BSA ≥ 2.0 m^2^) get a **lower** indexed flow, 1.8–2.0, to avoid high flow through the oxygenator.

Adequate for

topic: Changes During CPB: Total Systemic Blood Flow
stem: During CPB at conventional flow rates, the **mixed venous oxygen saturation is high**. Which interpretation is correct?

choices.text: It does not ensure cellular oxygenation if perfusion is uneven
It confirms that every tissue is receiving adequate oxygen
It shows that whole-body oxygen consumption is at requirement
It excludes lactic acidemia and metabolic acidosis
It proves that the capillary bed is evenly perfused

explanation.text: A high mixed venous PO~2~ or saturation ==does not mean cellular oxygenation is satisfactory==; an oxygen consumption at or near the whole-body requirement does.

steps.label: with Q and CaO~2~ fixed
steps.text: Mixed venous O~2~ **rises as VO~2~ falls**

steps.label: when the capillary bed is unevenly perfused
steps.text: Perfused capillaries are farther from many cells -> those cells go **hypoxic**

steps.label: amounts to
steps.text: A **shunt** of arterial blood into the venous system (sometimes half the total flow)

explanation.title: More flow is not the cure
explanation.text: If VO~2~ is below usual levels at conventional flow, increasing flow **probably will not** increase it: the fault is in the **capillary bed or at the cellular level**.

In this case, the distance between perfused capillaries and many tissue cells increases, and these cells do not obtain their oxygen requirement. This amounts to a shunt of arterial blood into the venous system.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 49

choiceNotes.b: A high mixed venous level does **not** mean cellular oxygenation is satisfactory; poorly perfused tissue may be hypoxic.
choiceNotes.c: Within the conventional flow range, mixed venous saturation is **inversely related** to oxygen consumption.
choiceNotes.d: Underperfused capillary beds produce **lactic acidemia and metabolic acidosis** despite these indices.
choiceNotes.e: Mixed venous oxygen **rises** when the capillary bed is unevenly perfused, as in a shunt.

topic: Changes During CPB: Arterial Pressure Waveform
stem: During cooling on CPB without a pulsatile pump, the team wants a **pulsatile arterial waveform**. How can this be achieved?

choices.text: Tighten the caval tapes and raise the venous reservoir vacuum
Set the arterial roller pump fully occlusive
Fibrillate the heart and vent the left ventricle
Leave caval tapes off and let the left ventricle eject
Lower the pump flow until arterial pressure becomes pulsatile

explanation.text: Pulsation can be achieved by ==partial CPB==: with no caval tapes, arterial flow is temporarily increased over venous return (or venous tubing partly occluded) so the **left ventricle ejects**.

steps.text: No tapes; arterial flow > venous return (or venous line partly occluded)

steps.label: so
steps.text: **Left ventricular ejection** adds to systemic flow

steps.label: giving
steps.text: Somewhat **pulsatile** arterial flow + some **pulmonary** blood flow

children: Partial CPB, during cooling and rewarming

explanation.title: Only if the heart can cope
explanation.text: Used whenever cardiac action is **vigorous enough to prevent overdistention** of the heart.
In other words, pulsation is achieved by partial CPB. This mechanism is used during cooling and rewarming whenever cardiac action is sufficiently vigorous to prevent overdistention of the heart.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 50

choiceNotes.a: Pulsation comes from **partial CPB**: caval tapes are left off and atrial filling is increased.
choiceNotes.b: The roller pump gives relatively **nonpulsatile** flow; full occlusion only increases blood trauma.
choiceNotes.c: Pulsation relies on **left ventricular ejection**, which needs sufficiently vigorous cardiac action.
choiceNotes.e: The method described **raises** arterial flow over venous return (or partly occludes venous tubing) to fill the heart.

topic: Changes During CPB: Arterial Pressure Waveform
stem: Which conclusion about **pulsatile versus nonpulsatile** flow during CPB is best supported?

choices.text: A randomized trial in moderate hypothermia found lower lactate with pulsatile flow
Pulsatile flow has been proven superior in infants
Nonpulsatile flow at 80 mmHg caused subendocardial ischemia in dog hearts
Pulsatile flow energy is usually reported as energy-equivalent pressure
Evidence that it importantly reduces CPB ill effects is insufficient

explanation.text: There is ==insufficient evidence== that pulsatile flow importantly reduces the ill effects of the relatively short CPB needed for most cardiac surgery.

head: Evidence
Finding
rows: Vascular resistance ↑, red cells aggregate, renal function impaired, renin released, cellular hypoxia -> metabolic acidosis
**No significant differences**; no evidence of better microcirculatory perfusion
Nonpulsatile at **50 mmHg** -> subendocardial ischemia; at **80 mmHg** none with either
Faster cooling/rewarming, more urine; **difficult to interpret**

explanation.title: Where it might matter
explanation.text: Pulsatile flow could prove beneficial at **lower flows** or in **desperately ill high-risk** patients (low cardiac output, acidosis, renal failure).

Currently, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that pulsatile flow from the pump-oxygenator importantly reduces the ill effects of the relatively short periods of CPB required for cardiac surgery in the great majority of patients.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 50

choiceNotes.a: Singh and colleagues found **no significant differences** in VO~2~, lactate, vascular resistance, urine flow, or thermal gradients.
choiceNotes.b: An advantage in infants is **possible but not proven**; the supporting study is difficult to interpret.
choiceNotes.c: Subendocardial ischemia occurred with nonpulsatile flow at **50 mmHg**; at **80 mmHg** neither mode caused it.
choiceNotes.d: There is an **almost universal failure** to describe pulsatile energy properly, such as by energy-equivalent pressure.

topic: Changes During CPB: Systemic Venous Pressure
stem: During **total CPB**, how should systemic (central) venous pressure be managed?

choices.text: Keep it at 10–15 mmHg to ensure good venous return
Keep it close to zero, and no more than 10 mmHg
Raise it with extra prime volume to improve organ perfusion
Use the smallest cannulae that fit snugly in the cavae
Lower it by increasing systemic blood flow

explanation.text: There is no physiologic advantage to a CVP above zero during total CPB; keep it ==close to zero, and certainly not more than 10 mmHg==, to minimize extracellular fluid increase.

explanation.caption: Equation 2-2: Pv = f(Q · viscosity / cannula size, tubing size, venous negative pressure)
head: Raises venous pressure
Lowers venous pressure
rows: Larger **venous cannulae** (their cross-sectional area and length are the main fixed factors)

explanation.title: With small cannulae
explanation.text: Reduce systemic blood flow or apply **suction to the venous return** (vacuum-assisted venous return) to keep venous pressure acceptable.
Venous pressure should, therefore, be kept close to zero, and certainly not more than 10 mmHg, to minimize increases in extracellular fluid.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 50

choiceNotes.a: Venous pressure should be **close to zero** and certainly not more than 10 mmHg.
choiceNotes.c: There is **no apparent physiologic advantage** to a CVP above zero; raising it needs more volume and often more prime.
choiceNotes.d: The **largest** venous cannulae compatible with the situation are used, lying **loosely, not snugly**.
choiceNotes.e: Venous pressure is a function of flow; with small cannulae, **reducing** flow (or applying venous suction) lowers it.

topic: Changes During CPB: Pulmonary Venous Pressure
stem: During total CPB, left atrial pressure monitoring shows **rising pulmonary venous pressure**. Which decompression method is effective?

choices.text: More vacuum on the venous reservoir via the caval cannulae
Waiting until the pressure exceeds 20 mmHg
Suction via a catheter in the pulmonary trunk
Increasing arterial pump flow to the patient
Lowering plasma colloid osmotic pressure with crystalloid

explanation.text: The pulmonary venous system can be decompressed by suction on a catheter (or opening) ==in the pulmonary trunk, because pulmonary veins have no valves==, or by a catheter in the left atrium or left ventricle.

explanation.title: Not a guarantee
explanation.text: Maintaining a very low pulmonary venous pressure **will not always** eliminate these complications.

the pulmonary venous system can be decompressed by suction on either a catheter (or an opening) in the pulmonary trunk, because no valves are present in pulmonary veins, or a catheter inside the left atrium or left ventricle.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 51

choiceNotes.a: Venous vacuum drains **systemic** venous return; pulmonary venous decompression uses the pulmonary trunk, left atrium, or left ventricle.
choiceNotes.b: Pulmonary venous pressure should ideally be **zero** and certainly not more than **10 mmHg**; lung water rises with the duration of elevation.
choiceNotes.d: Raising arterial flow over venous return **increases** atrial filling pressures.
choiceNotes.e: By the Starling law, a lower plasma colloid osmotic pressure favors **more** fluid moving out of the capillaries.

stem: During core cooling, blood entering the aorta is kept **no more than 10°C–14°C below** the nasopharyngeal temperature. What is the reason?

choices.text: To prevent blood damage at the heat exchanger surface
To prevent red cell aggregation in cold, sluggish flow
To limit gas coming out of solution on warming
To keep Tygon tubing from losing its elasticity
To limit the oxygen transfer demand on the oxygenator

explanation.text: Cold blood warmed by the patient tends to ==release dissolved gas==; keeping arterial blood no more than **10°C–14°C** below nasopharyngeal temperature minimizes this.
This is a **conservative** recommendation: some groups use the coldest perfusate obtainable (**4°C–5°C**) once CPB is started.

blood entering the patient’s aorta should be kept no greater than 10°C to 14°C below the nasopharyngeal temperature to minimize the tendency for gas to come out of solution when the cold blood is warmed by the patient.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 51

choiceNotes.a: Heat-exchanger blood damage concerns temperatures **above 42°C** during rewarming.
choiceNotes.b: Rouleaux are addressed by a **lower hematocrit** at low temperature, not by this gradient.
choiceNotes.d: Tygon stiffening is managed by using **silicone rubber** tubing in the pump head.
choiceNotes.e: Maximal oxygenator demand occurs during **rewarming**, not cooling.

stem: During **rewarming** on CPB, which statement about the heat exchanger and gas in the blood is correct?

choices.text: A downstream heat exchanger may need a bubble trap in the arterial tubing
An upstream heat exchanger is the position that risks bubble formation
Warming the blood increases the solubility of gas within it
Water may exceed 42°C, since only blood temperature matters at the wall
An exchanger-to-blood gradient of up to 20°C avoids bubble formation

explanation.text: Warming ==lowers gas solubility== in blood. This is not a problem with the heat exchanger **upstream** of the oxygenator, but **downstream** it is a potential problem, and a **bubble trap** may be interposed in the arterial tubing downstream to both.

head: Heat exchanger position
During rewarming
rows: Potential bubble problem -> **bubble trap** in the arterial tubing

steps.label: and
steps.text: The boundary layer at the exchanger wall probably reaches the **wall (water) temperature**

explanation.title: Gradient rule
explanation.text: In general, a heat exchanger-to-blood temperature gradient of **not more than 10°C–12°C** prevents bubble formation.
Solubility of gas in blood is decreased when blood is warmed, but this is not a problem when the heat exchanger is upstream (proximal) to the oxygenator.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 51

choiceNotes.b: Decreased gas solubility on warming is **not a problem** when the heat exchanger is **upstream** (proximal) to the oxygenator.
choiceNotes.c: Solubility of gas in blood is **decreased** when blood is warmed.
choiceNotes.d: The boundary layer of blood probably reaches the wall (water) temperature, and blood is damaged above **42°C**, so water should not exceed 42°C.
choiceNotes.e: In general, a gradient of **not more than 10°C–12°C** from the heat exchanger to the blood prevents bubble formation.
